prompt: Why does every check this course added make the pipeline more attractive to an attacker?

choices.text: Scanners publish their findings where anyone can read them
choices.why: The findings stay in the run's logs; the attraction is the credentials.

choices.text: Each one is a job that holds credentials
choices.why: Right. Running a line of your choosing in that job gets them all: tokens, registry access and the signing key are in the job for its whole length.

choices.text: More stages make every run slower
choices.why: Speed is lesson 2's concern; it does not attract anybody.

choices.text: The tools are downloaded from the internet on every run
choices.why: This course installs each tool once, checked; the point is what a job holds.

prompt: In the tj-actions/changed-files incident of 2025, which workflows ran the altered code?

choices.text: Those that named the action by a commit hash
choices.why: A commit hash cannot be moved, so those workflows kept running the old code.

choices.text: Only workflows on self-hosted runners
choices.why: The runner type did not matter; the tag did.

choices.text: Those that named it by a version tag
choices.why: Right. The tags were moved to a new commit, and every run that resolved them took it.

choices.text: Those that used `pull_request_target` as their trigger
choices.why: The trigger was not what decided it; the reference to the action was.

prompt: Match each party to how it can influence what a CI job runs.

pairs.right: the code the job checks out
the commit a tag points at
the machine the job runs on

prompt: How many findings did zizmor report on the careless workflow with its default persona?
Why is `pull_request_target` combined with a checkout of the pull request's head the dangerous pair, rather than either alone?

choices.text: The checkout runs a stranger's code with the trigger's privileges
choices.why: Right. The trigger grants a write token and secrets. Alone, the trigger runs the base branch's code; alone, the checkout runs under a read-only token.

choices.text: Checking out a fork is slower under that trigger
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; privileges are.

choices.text: The trigger disables the template-injection protection of GitHub
choices.why: There is no such protection to disable; injection is a separate finding.

choices.text: The head commit is unsigned, and GitHub refuses unsigned commits there
choices.why: GitHub runs unsigned commits; signature is not the risk here.

prompt: What makes `${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}` inside `run:` a code injection?

choices.text: The title is sent to GitHub's API without encryption
choices.why: Transport is not the issue; where the text lands is.

choices.text: The text becomes part of the script
choices.why: Right. It is expanded before the shell parses the script, so whatever the author typed becomes part of the program; an environment variable keeps it a value.

choices.text: The title is longer than the shell's line limit
choices.why: Length is not the danger; meaning is.

choices.text: `echo` prints secrets when given a title
choices.why: `echo` prints what it is given; the problem is that the title is code by then.

prompt: zizmor's default persona did not report `permissions: write-all`; the `auditor` persona did. What does the lesson take from that?

choices.text: `write-all` is harmless on a pull request workflow
choices.why: It hands the job a token that can write; the default persona's silence is a tuning choice.

choices.text: The default persona is broken and should not be used
choices.why: It is tuned for few false positives, which is why it is the pipeline's default.

choices.text: Read a new workflow as an auditor first, then rely on the default
choices.why: Right. The default stays quiet on purpose; a deliberate first pass looks at everything.

choices.text: The auditor persona needs network access to work
choices.why: Both ran with `--offline`.

prompt: `git ls-remote` showed `v6` and `v6.1.0` naming the same commit. Which one is pinned in the workflow, and how?

choices.text: `v6`, because it receives fixes automatically
choices.why: Receiving changes automatically is exactly what a pin refuses.

choices.text: The commit hash, with `# v6.1.0` beside it
choices.why: Right. The hash cannot move, and the comment tells the reader and the update bots which release it is.

choices.text: `v6.1.0`, because an exact version tag cannot move
choices.why: Any tag can be moved by whoever controls the repository.

choices.text: Both, so either can be used as a fallback
choices.why: A workflow names one reference per step.

prompt: `actions/checkout` writes the job's token into `.git/config` unless the step sets `persist-credentials: ___`.
Why declare `permissions: contents: read` in the file instead of relying on the repository's default?

choices.text: A line in the file is reviewed with the code
choices.why: Right. A repository setting changes with no review. The file makes the job's privileges part of what a reviewer reads.

choices.text: The repository default is always write-all
choices.why: The default is whatever the repository or organisation set; the file makes it independent of that.

choices.text: zizmor cannot read repository settings
choices.why: True offline, but the reason the lesson gives is review, not the scanner.

choices.text: GITHUB_TOKEN does not exist unless permissions are declared
choices.why: The token exists for every job; the declaration limits it.

prompt: Why does `workflows` run second in `ci/stages`, before the tests?

choices.text: zizmor needs the image that the build stage makes
choices.why: zizmor reads text files; it needs no image.

choices.text: It is cheap, reads only text, and fails ahead of the costly work
choices.why: Right: it fails before the costly stages, the same reason `secrets` is first.

choices.text: The tests would overwrite `.github` if they ran first
choices.why: Nothing in the tests touches `.github`.

choices.text: GitHub requires workflow files to be checked before tests
choices.why: GitHub requires nothing of this local CI.

prompt: The branch `title-in-run` stopped at the `workflows` stage. What did not happen as a result?

choices.text: The commit was not recorded in the CI's repository
choices.why: The push was accepted; the run is what stopped.

choices.text: zizmor did not print the line of the finding
choices.why: It printed the finding with the line.

choices.text: The pre-commit hook did not scan the change for secrets
choices.why: The hook ran at commit time, before the push.

choices.text: No image was built, pushed or signed
choices.why: Right. The pipeline stops at the first failure, so nothing reached the registry.

prompt: Which risk does `zizmor --offline` leave unchecked that its online audits would cover?

choices.text: A `run:` step that expands a pull request's title
choices.why: That is template injection, found offline from the file.

choices.text: A pinned hash that does not belong to the action it names
choices.why: Right: the impostor-commit audit needs GitHub's API.

choices.text: An action referenced by a tag
choices.why: `unpinned-uses` found that offline, twice.

choices.text: A checkout that keeps the token in `.git/config`
choices.why: `artipacked` found that offline.

prompt: What does a persistent runner allow that an ephemeral one does not?

choices.text: Running jobs from more than one repository
choices.why: Both kinds can serve several repositories; lifetime is the difference.

choices.text: A job leaving something on disk that the next job runs on top of
choices.why: Right. Caches, tools and processes survive, so one job can poison every later one.

choices.text: Using a token with read-only permissions
choices.why: Token permissions come from the workflow, not the runner's lifetime.

choices.text: Running a workflow on `pull_request`
choices.why: Both kinds run any trigger.

prompt: A public repository's workflow uses `pull_request` with a read-only token and no secrets, on a self-hosted runner in the office network. What is still exposed?

choices.text: The repository's contents, through the read-only token
choices.why: Read-only on a public repository exposes nothing that is not already public.

choices.text: The repository's secrets
choices.why: `pull_request` from a fork withholds them.

choices.text: Nothing, because the trigger is the safe one
choices.why: The trigger protects the repository, not the machine the stranger's code runs on.

choices.text: The runner machine and whatever it reaches on the network
choices.why: Right. A fork's code runs there, inside the office network.

prompt: Which two facts on screen establish that a CI stage on this laptop can act as root?

choices.text: `id` shows the docker group; the group writes to the socket
choices.why: Right. With the daemon running as root, write access to its socket is root.

choices.text: The CI runs as ana, and ana owns `~/ci`
choices.why: Owning a directory gives power over that directory, not over the host.

choices.text: ana has a password, and `sudo` is installed
choices.why: Neither appeared on screen, and neither is the path the lesson names.

choices.text: The registry listens on localhost, and Docker built the image
choices.why: Neither says who can control the daemon.

prompt: What does rootless Docker change about access to the daemon's socket?

choices.text: It removes the socket, so nobody can talk to the daemon
choices.why: The socket moves to the user's runtime directory; it still exists.

choices.text: It encrypts the socket with the user's password
choices.why: There is no such encryption; the change is who the daemon runs as.

choices.text: Access to the socket is worth the user's rights, not root's
choices.why: Right. The daemon runs as that user, inside a user namespace.

choices.text: It lets containers bind ports below 1024 without configuration
choices.why: The documentation lists low ports as a limitation that needs extra configuration.

prompt: Put the links of the chain that makes a pushed branch as powerful as root on this laptop in order, from the push.
items: the hook runs the commit's own stage scripts
ana is in the docker group
the group can write to the daemon's socket

prompt: A team moves linkbox to GitHub with this lesson's workflow and adds a release job that signs images with a key stored as a repository secret. Which control from lesson 14 and this lesson does that job still need most?

choices.text: Running zizmor with the `auditor` persona on every push
choices.why: Worth doing, but it does not keep the key away from the job's own steps.

choices.text: No step of the job reads the key
choices.why: Right: sign outside the job's steps, or keyless with the workflow's identity. That is what separates L2 from L3, and it removes the long-lived secret.

choices.text: Pinning `ubuntu-24.04` instead of `ubuntu-latest`
choices.why: That fixes the runner image's version, not who can use the key.

choices.text: Adding `concurrency` so two releases never overlap
choices.why: Overlap is a reliability concern; the key is still readable by every step.

prompt: A pull request changes `ci/workflows.sh` to `zizmor --offline .github || true`. What should a reviewer conclude?

choices.text: It is a speed improvement for the stage
choices.why: It changes the verdict, not the speed.

choices.text: It is harmless, because the findings still appear in the log
choices.why: A finding nobody is stopped by is a finding nobody reads, as lesson 7 argued.

choices.text: It is needed so that warnings are counted
choices.why: Warnings in this pipeline are exit status 3, which this change would also hide.

choices.text: A commit has switched the check off
choices.why: Right. The stage no longer fails. Because stages come from the commit, review is where this is caught.

prompt: Which of these changes are part of the fixed workflow? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: permissions reduced to contents: read
choices.why: Yes: the token can read the repository and nothing else.

choices.text: each action pinned to a commit, with its version in a comment
choices.why: Yes: a tag can be moved, a commit cannot.

choices.text: the pull request's title passed through an environment variable
choices.why: Yes: the shell reads it as data, never as code.

choices.text: pull_request_target kept, so forks get the repository's secrets
choices.why: No: that trigger with a checkout of the head is what made the old workflow dangerous.

choices.text: the checkout keeps its credentials for later steps
choices.why: No: persist-credentials is set to false so no later step finds the token on disk.
